Stage 3 · Language

Asking without sounding blunt

Indirect questions, and how to stop repeating yourself.

Read these four lines from two phone calls.
  • I wonder if you could check for me?
  • Could you tell me the opening hours, please?
  • Do I need to take a towel with me, or are they provided?
  • I wonder if I could come and pick it up this evening?
What do all four have in common?
A direct question can sound abrupt. English has a longer, safer way of asking.

When you ask a stranger or a business for information, a bare direct question — How much is it? — is grammatically fine but socially thin. English prefers to wrap the question inside a longer frame: Could you tell me how much it is? The extra words signal that you know you are asking a favour, and they are standard in phone enquiries, service encounters and written requests.

The frame changes the grammar of what follows, and this is the part that has to be learnt carefully. An indirect question is no longer a question in structure — it is a statement inside a question. So the subject goes back in front of the verb, and any do, does or did simply disappears. What time does it open? becomes Could you tell me what time it opens? The auxiliary is not moved somewhere else; it is deleted, because its only job was to build the direct question.

Yes/no questions have no question word to introduce the clause, so English supplies one: if or whether. Is breakfast included? becomes Could you tell me whether breakfast is included? In formal writing whether is the safer choice, and it is obligatory directly before or not.

The second half of this lesson deals with a different problem: repetition. A short enquiry that says room six times reads as clumsy. English avoids this with substitution — one and ones replace a countable noun (a quieter one), do so replaces a whole verb phrase in formal writing, and this, that and there point back at a whole idea. Using these well is one of the clearest markers of competent written English at this level.

Before you look at the table: the table below shows the transformation from direct to indirect question side by side. Watch what happens to the auxiliary in each pair — that is the rule the whole lesson turns on.
The wrapper, and the word order inside it
Direct questionPolite versionWhat changed
What is the price?Could you tell me what the price is?the verb moves after the subject
Do you have a gym?Could you tell me whether you have a gym?yes/no question → whether or if, no do
When does it open?Do you happen to know when it opens?no does, and the verb takes the ending
Check it for me.I wonder if you could check it for me.an order becomes a question
Not repeating yourself
Instead of repeatingUseExample
a singular nounoneI’d like a single room — a quiet one, if possible.
a plural nounonesThe cheap rooms are gone, so I’ll take one of the expensive ones.
a whole actiondo so / do thatYou may cancel free of charge if you do so before Friday.
a whole ideathis / thatThe price rose in June. That was not mentioned on the website.
a placethereWe stayed at the Grand. My parents got married there.

The polite opening does the work. What time do you open? is not rude, but Could you tell me what time you open? is the version that gets a full answer from a stranger.

Inside the wrapper, the question stops being a question. No do, no does, no did, and the subject comes before the verb — exactly like a normal sentence.

The mistake to avoid. Not Could you tell me what is the price? but Could you tell me what the price is? This is the single error that marks an enquiry as non-native.

Whether or if? Both work in speech. In formal writing, whether is safer, and it is the only one possible before or not: whether or not it is included.

Full grammar reference — making enquiries, and avoiding repetition

What it is

Two things a good enquiry needs. First, the indirect question forms English uses to ask for information politely — Could you tell me whether…?, I’d be grateful if you could…, Do you happen to know…? Second, the substitution devices that stop a request from repeating itself: one / ones, do so, and the pointers this, that, there, so.

What it means, and what it does

A bare direct question can sound abrupt in a request to a stranger or a business: How much is it? is not wrong, but Could you tell me how much it is? signals that you know you are asking a favour. The longer form buys goodwill. Substitution then keeps the message readable: an email that says room six times reads as clumsy, while a double room … a quieter one … if that is possible reads as competent English.

When and why we use it

When you ask a stranger or a business for information, a bare direct question — How much is it? — is grammatically fine but socially thin. English prefers to wrap the question inside a longer frame: Could you tell me how much it is? The extra words signal that you know you are asking a favour, and they are standard in phone enquiries, service encounters and written requests.

The frame changes the grammar of what follows, and this is the part that has to be learnt carefully. An indirect question is no longer a question in structure — it is a statement inside a question. So the subject goes back in front of the verb, and any do, does or did simply disappears. What time does it open? becomes Could you tell me what time it opens? The auxiliary is not moved somewhere else; it is deleted, because its only job was to build the direct question.

Yes/no questions have no question word to introduce the clause, so English supplies one: if or whether. Is breakfast included? becomes Could you tell me whether breakfast is included? In formal writing whether is the safer choice, and it is obligatory directly before or not.

The second half of this lesson deals with a different problem: repetition. A short enquiry that says room six times reads as clumsy. English avoids this with substitution — one and ones replace a countable noun (a quieter one), do so replaces a whole verb phrase in formal writing, and this, that and there point back at a whole idea. Using these well is one of the clearest markers of competent written English at this level.

Typical situations

You need this language for phoning a hotel, a gym or a restaurant, writing an enquiry email, asking about a course or a price, and generally asking anything of somebody you do not know.

  • Asking for information politely — the indirect question, spoken or written.Could you tell me whether breakfast is included?
  • Opening a written enquiry — the fixed formula that starts an enquiry email.I am writing to enquire about your weekend rates.
  • Making a request — I’d be grateful if you could… is the standard formal request.I’d be grateful if you could confirm the price per person.
  • Softening an unlikely question — Do you happen to know…? lowers the pressure to answer.Do you happen to know if there’s parking nearby?
  • Closing an enquiry — the fixed sign-off before the name.I look forward to hearing from you.
  • Avoiding a repeated noun — one for singular countable, ones for plural.We have a standard room and a larger one.
  • Avoiding a repeated verb phrase — do so in formal writing; do in speech.Please book by Friday; if you fail to do so, the price rises.
  • Pointing back at a whole idea — this, that, there, so.The hotel is fully booked. If that is the case, we’ll try elsewhere.

How it differs from similar structures

Could you tell me…? (polite request for information) · Do you happen to know…? (softer, implies they may not know) · I’d be grateful if you could… (formal, asks for an action, not just information).
if and whether are usually interchangeable, but only whether works before or not and before to + verb: whether to book now or wait.

How to build it

Indirect question, wh-: Could you tell me + wh-word + subject + verb  (statement order)
Indirect question, yes/no: Could you tell me + if / whether + subject + verb
Formal request: I’d be grateful if you could + base verb
Substitution: a / the + adjective + one  ·  verb phrase → do so
Direct → indirect, wh-What time does it open? → Could you tell me what time it opens?
Direct → indirect, yes/noIs breakfast included? → Could you tell me whether breakfast is included?
No do / does / didCould you tell me what time does it open? — the auxiliary disappears.
Word ordersubject before verb, exactly as in a statement: …how much it costs, not how much costs it.
PunctuationA question mark only if the whole sentence is a question: Could you tell me…? but I’d like to know… takes a full stop.
one / onesthe cheap one · the cheaper ones — never with uncountable nouns.
do soHe asked me to confirm and I did so immediately.

Usage notes and exceptions

  • Whether is safer than if in formal writing, and it is obligatory before or not placed directly after it: whether or not it is available, not if or not.
  • The auxiliary do / does / did is deleted, not moved, when a question becomes indirect. This is the error learners make most often here and it recurs in reported questions (Lesson 35).
  • One replaces a countable noun only. With uncountables, repeat nothing at all: I’d like some water — cold, please, not a cold one.
  • One needs a determiner or adjective in front of it: the blue one, a bigger one. On its own after some or a number, use nothing or ones: I’ll take three.
  • Do so is formal and written; in speech English simply drops the phrase or uses do it. Do so in a text message sounds odd.
  • Register consistency matters: I am writing to enquire and Cheers do not belong in the same email. Choose formal throughout or neutral throughout.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • Could you tell me what time does the pool open? → Could you tell me what time the pool opens?The auxiliary does is deleted in an indirect question.
  • I am writing for enquire about your rates. → I am writing to enquire about your rates.The formula takes the infinitive with to.
  • Could you tell me is breakfast included? → Could you tell me whether breakfast is included?A yes/no question needs if or whether.
  • I would be grateful if you could to confirm. → I would be grateful if you could confirm.Could is a modal and takes the base verb.
  • We have a single room and a double. → We have a single room and a double one.One is needed after an adjective replacing a countable noun.
  • I look forward to hear from you. → I look forward to hearing from you.Look forward to is followed by -ing.

More examples in context

  • openingI am writing to enquire about availability for the last weekend in May.
  • indirect wh-Could you tell me what the rate is per person?
  • indirect yes/noI’d like to know whether the price includes breakfast.
  • formal requestI’d be grateful if you could send me a confirmation by email.
  • soft enquiryDo you happen to know if there’s a later ferry?
  • substitution — oneWe saw two flats; the second one was much quieter.
  • substitution — onesI’ll take the cheaper ones, please.
  • substitution — do soGuests must check out by eleven; those who fail to do so are charged.
  • pointerThe room is on the top floor. Is that a problem for you?
  • closingThank you in advance. I look forward to hearing from you.

A tip for remembering it

Convert a direct question in two moves and you will never get the word order wrong. Move 1: delete do / does / did. Move 2: put the subject in front of the verb, as in a statement. What does it cost? → delete does → what it costs → Could you tell me what it costs?

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. Indirect questions use statement word order: subject before verb.
  2. Delete do / does / did when you make a question indirect.
  3. Yes/no questions need if or whether; use whether before or not.
  4. A question mark only if the whole sentence is a question.
  5. One / ones replace countable nouns after an adjective or determiner.
  6. Do so replaces a repeated verb phrase in formal writing; keep the register consistent throughout the email.

Stage 5 · Main input

An email that gets answered

Read it as a writer. You are going to write one like it.

Before you read: what makes a company answer an email quickly?

Choose one. Then count how many of the four the model does.

Subject: Enquiry about summer courses

Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to enquire about the summer English courses advertised on your website.

Could you tell me whether any places are still available in July? I would also be grateful if you could confirm the total cost per week, and whether that price includes accommodation.

Two further questions. First, do you happen to know how many students there are in each group? Second, if I book now, is it possible to change the dates later?

I am attaching a copy of my most recent language certificate, in case it is useful.

I look forward to hearing from you.

Yours faithfully,
Aizhan Serikova

What the model does, in five moves
  • Says why in one sentence, before anything else.
  • Groups the questions so the reader can answer them one by one.
  • Wraps every question — Could you tell me whether…, not Do you have…?
  • Offers something the reader has not asked for yet.
  • Closes with one fixed line and the right sign-off. Dear Sir or Madam goes with Yours faithfully; a name goes with Yours sincerely.
